title: Best interests, LPAs, advance decisions and advocacy
blurb: Make best interests decisions with the s4 checklist, and know when an LPA, an advance decision or an IMCA changes who decides.
question: Mr Shah, 69, has motor neurone disease and now lacks capacity. He has a signed, witnessed document refusing ventilation, but it does not say it applies even if his life is at risk. The team is considering ventilation. Is the refusal binding?

teach.h: When the person can't decide, someone must decide well
teach.body: Once a person has been assessed as lacking capacity for a decision, anything done for them must be in their best interests (MCA s1(5)), and the less restrictive option must be considered (s1(6)). But first ask: has the person already made the decision (a valid advance decision), or appointed someone to make it (a lasting power of attorney)? In plain English: their own earlier choice comes first, then their chosen attorney, then a best interests decision.

steps.sub: Decision maker uses the s4 checklist

head: s4
The decision maker must...
rows: Not decide merely on age, appearance, condition or behaviour
Consider whether and when the person may regain capacity
Encourage the person to participate as fully as possible
For life-sustaining treatment, not be motivated by a desire to bring about death
Consider past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values
Consult named people, carers, any attorney or deputy
teach.caption: s4(6)(a) gives particular weight to any relevant written statement made when the person had capacity.
s9(2)(b): an LPA is not created unless registered. s11(7)-(8): welfare authority applies when the person lacks capacity.

rows.label: Signed
values: Signed by P, or for P in P's presence

rows.label: Statement
values: "Applies even if life is at risk"

teach.caption: s24-25. A person with capacity can withdraw an ADRT at any time; the withdrawal need not be in writing.

teach.body: Mr Shah's document is written, signed and witnessed, but it lacks the statement that it applies even if his life is at risk. Under s25(5)-(6) it therefore cannot apply to life-sustaining treatment such as ventilation. It is still powerful evidence of his wishes, which the decision maker must consider under s4(6)(a). The team makes a best interests decision, consulting his family and anyone he named, and records how his wishes were weighed.

teach.h: IMCA: a voice for people with nobody else
teach.body: An independent mental capacity advocate represents a person who lacks capacity when there is nobody appropriate to consult other than paid carers. An NHS body must instruct an IMCA before providing serious medical treatment (s37) and before arranging hospital or care home accommodation (s38), unless the matter is urgent. The local authority must do so for longer-term residential moves of 8 weeks or more (s39). The decision maker must take the IMCA's information into account.

It is a criminal offence for a person caring for someone who lacks capacity (or an attorney or deputy) to ill-treat or wilfully neglect them. The maximum penalty on indictment is 5 years' imprisonment. A nurse who sees this must act to protect the person and raise it as a safeguarding concern (Code 17.1).

teach.text: An ADRT made BEFORE an LPA is overridden for that treatment if the later LPA gives the attorney authority over it (s25(2)(b)). A property and financial affairs LPA gives NO authority over medical treatment. And 'next of kin' has no legal power to consent for an adult.

items: Order: valid ADRT, then health and welfare attorney or deputy, then best interests decision.
s4 checklist: no assumptions, regain capacity?, participation, wishes and values, consult others.
ADRT refusing life-sustaining treatment: written, signed, witnessed, 'even if life is at risk'.
LPA must be registered; a welfare attorney refuses life-sustaining treatment only if expressly authorised.
IMCA when nobody appropriate to consult; s44 offence of ill-treatment or wilful neglect (5 years).

summary: You can now work out who has the authority to decide for someone who lacks capacity, check whether an advance decision or LPA is valid and applicable, apply the s4 best interests checklist, and recognise when an IMCA is needed or a s44 offence may have occurred.

A.q: Mrs Price, 88, has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to decide about a feeding tube. The team is making a best interests decision. What must they consider?
options: What most patients of her age would choose in this particular situation
The treatment the consultant judges clinically most effective
Her past wishes, beliefs and values, as reported by those close to her
What her son, as next of kin, decides would be the best choice
A.why: MCA s4(6): consider the person's past and present wishes and feelings, beliefs and values; s4(7): consult carers and others interested in her welfare about what she would want.

whyNot.0: s4(1) prohibits deciding merely on age, and best interests is about her, not a typical patient.
whyNot.1: Clinical effectiveness is relevant but best interests is wider than medical judgement.
whyNot.3: Her son must be consulted, but next of kin has no legal power to decide.

A.q: Ms Douglas, 55, has capacity. Last year she made a valid advance decision refusing antibiotics for pneumonia. Today she tells the nurse she no longer wants it to apply. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask her to put the withdrawal in writing and have it witnessed
Check with her family before recording any change to it
Explain it stays in force until her solicitor cancels it
Accept the withdrawal and document it clearly in her records
A.why: MCA s24(3)-(4): a person with capacity may withdraw an advance decision at any time, and a withdrawal need not be in writing. The nurse records it and informs the team.

whyNot.0: A withdrawal does not need to be written or witnessed.
whyNot.1: She has capacity; her family's agreement is not required.
whyNot.2: No solicitor is needed to withdraw an advance decision.

A.q: Mr Fox, 82, lacks capacity to consent to a hip operation. His nephew produces a registered LPA for property and financial affairs and says he will consent. What is the correct position?
options: The nephew can consent, as the LPA has been registered
The nephew can consent if Mr Fox's GP agrees to it
This type of LPA does not cover medical treatment
The operation cannot proceed until a deputy is appointed
A.why: MCA s9(1) distinguishes personal welfare (health and welfare) LPAs from property and affairs LPAs. A financial attorney has no authority over treatment, so the decision is made in Mr Fox's best interests, consulting his nephew.

whyNot.0: Registration validates the LPA, but this type does not cover health decisions.
whyNot.1: A GP's agreement cannot extend a financial LPA to treatment.
whyNot.3: A best interests decision can be made without a deputy.

B.q: Mrs Kowalski, 79, lacks capacity to decide about a move to long-term residential care. She has no family, friends or unpaid carers. Who must be instructed to represent her?
options: An independent mental capacity advocate
Her GP, as the professional who knows her best
The care home manager who will receive her
A Court of Protection-appointed deputy
B.why: MCA ss35, 38-39: where there is nobody appropriate to consult other than paid carers, an IMCA must be instructed for long-term accommodation decisions (unless urgent).

whyNot.1: Her GP is involved professionally and cannot act as her independent representative.
whyNot.2: The receiving manager has an interest in the outcome and is not independent.
whyNot.3: A deputy is not needed; the Act provides IMCAs for exactly this situation.

B.q: A healthcare assistant in a care home in England has repeatedly left Mr Garner, who lacks capacity, in a soiled bed without food. What is the legal significance?
options: It is an employment matter for the home manager to resolve
It is a civil matter that his family may choose to pursue
It is poor practice that should be addressed by retraining
It may be a criminal offence of wilful neglect under s44
B.why: MCA s44: ill-treatment or wilful neglect of a person lacking capacity by someone caring for them is an offence; maximum 5 years' imprisonment on indictment. It is also a safeguarding concern (Code 17.1).

whyNot.0: It may be a disciplinary matter too, but the law treats it as a possible crime.
whyNot.1: It is not limited to a civil claim; s44 creates a criminal offence.
whyNot.2: Retraining does not address a possible criminal offence or protect Mr Garner.

B.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to resolve. What should they do?
options: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Decide now in her best interests to speed up her discharge
Ask her daughter to make the decision on her behalf
Apply to the Court of Protection for a quick decision
B.why: MCA s4(3): consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and when. If the decision can wait, it should, so she can make it herself.

whyNot.1: Discharge pressure does not justify deciding for her when she may soon decide herself.
whyNot.2: Her daughter has no legal authority without an LPA or deputyship.
whyNot.3: Court involvement is unnecessary when the decision can simply wait.

C.q: Mr Shah, 69, lacks capacity. He made a written, signed and witnessed advance decision refusing ventilation, but it has no statement that it applies even if his life is at risk. What is its effect?
options: It is binding, because it is written, signed and properly witnessed
It is binding for 12 months after the date it was signed
It is binding if his family confirm it reflects his views
It is not valid as a refusal of this life-sustaining treatment
C.why: MCA s25(5)-(6): a refusal of life-sustaining treatment must include a statement that it applies even if life is at risk. Without it, it does not bind for ventilation, though it is strong evidence of his wishes for a best interests decision (s4(6)(a)).

whyNot.0: Writing, signature and witness are needed, but the 'even if life is at risk' statement is also required.
whyNot.1: Advance decisions have no fixed expiry period under the Act.
whyNot.2: Family confirmation cannot supply a missing statutory requirement.

C.q: Mr Okonjo, 74, lacks capacity after a cardiac arrest. He has a valid, applicable advance decision refusing CPR, meeting all s25 formalities. His daughter demands that he be resuscitated if he arrests again. What should the nurse do?
options: Follow the daughter's wishes, as she is his next of kin
Ask the consultant to decide in his best interests instead
Follow the advance decision and support his daughter
Seek an urgent IMCA before any decision is recorded
C.why: A valid and applicable advance decision has the same effect as a refusal made with capacity at the time (MCA s26(1)). Relatives cannot override it; the nurse explains this sensitively and supports her.

whyNot.0: Next of kin has no legal power to override a valid advance decision.
whyNot.1: Best interests does not apply where a valid, applicable ADRT already decides the matter.
whyNot.3: An IMCA is not needed; the decision has already been made by Mr Okonjo.

C.q: Ms Bryant, 61, lacks capacity. Her registered health and welfare LPA does not expressly cover life-sustaining treatment. Her attorney asks the team to stop her antibiotics for severe pneumonia. What is the position?
options: The attorney cannot refuse this life-sustaining treatment
The attorney's refusal is binding, as the LPA is registered
The attorney's refusal stands once two doctors have agreed
The attorney may refuse it after consulting an IMCA first
C.why: MCA s11(8)(a): a welfare attorney cannot refuse life-sustaining treatment unless the LPA contains express provision to that effect. The team decides in her best interests, consulting the attorney (s4(7)).

whyNot.1: Registration alone does not give authority over life-sustaining treatment.
whyNot.2: Medical agreement cannot create authority the LPA does not contain.
whyNot.3: With an attorney to consult, the IMCA duty does not arise, and an IMCA cannot extend the LPA.

reteach.title: Their voice, then their chosen voice, then the best guess at their voice
reteach.question: If a person can no longer speak for themselves, how do we still hear them?

blocks.h: Three ways the person is heard
blocks.body: Their own voice: a valid advance decision, made at 18+ with capacity, is followed as if they said it today. Their chosen voice: an attorney they appointed (registered health and welfare LPA). The best guess at their voice: a best interests decision built on their wishes, beliefs and values, what people close to them say, and their participation. If there is nobody to speak for them, an IMCA is appointed.

blocks.text: An advance STATEMENT of wishes ("I'd like music and to stay at home") must be considered but is not binding; an advance DECISION refusing treatment is binding if valid and applicable.

explain.body: No assumptions from age or condition; consider whether capacity may return; involve the person; weigh their wishes, beliefs and values; consult carers, named people, attorneys and deputies; never be motivated by a desire to bring about death.

test.q: Which is a required step in a best interests decision under s4?
options: Following the next of kin's choice
Deciding as the majority of patients would
Choosing the cheapest suitable option available
Consulting carers about the person's wishes
test.why: s4(7): take into account the views of carers and others interested in the person's welfare, particularly about the person's wishes.

whyNot.0: Relatives are consulted; they do not decide.
whyNot.1: The decision is about this person, not a typical patient.
whyNot.2: Cost is not the test; the person's best interests are.

explain.body: Two types: health and welfare; property and financial affairs. Not created until registered (s9(2)(b)). A welfare attorney acts only when the person lacks capacity, and refuses life-sustaining treatment only if expressly authorised (s11).

test.q: A daughter shows an unregistered health and welfare LPA. Can she consent to her father's treatment?
options: Yes, the signed document is enough
Yes, if two witnesses signed it
No, it must be registered first
No, an LPA does not cover treatment
test.why: MCA s9(2)(b): an LPA is not created unless it is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian.

whyNot.0: Signing does not create the LPA; registration does.
whyNot.3: A registered health and welfare LPA can cover treatment.

explain.body: Made at 18+ with capacity; can be withdrawn at any time, not necessarily in writing. For life-sustaining treatment: written, signed, witnessed, and stating it applies even if life is at risk (s24-25). Valid and applicable: same effect as a decision made now (s26).

test.q: Which is NOT required for an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment?
options: It is signed by a doctor
It is witnessed
It is in writing
It says it applies even if life is at risk
test.why: s25(6) requires writing, P's signature (or another's in P's presence at P's direction), a witness, and the 'even if life is at risk' statement. A doctor's signature is not required.

explain.body: An IMCA represents a person lacking capacity with nobody appropriate to consult, for serious medical treatment and accommodation moves (s35-39). s44 makes ill-treatment or wilful neglect a crime, up to 5 years.

test.q: When must an NHS body instruct an IMCA for serious medical treatment?
options: When the family disagree with the doctors' plan
When there is nobody appropriate to consult
When the person has a registered LPA
When the person is aged over 65
test.why: s37: an IMCA must be instructed where there is no person, other than paid or professional carers, whom it would be appropriate to consult.

whyNot.0: Family disagreement does not trigger the IMCA duty; there are people to consult.
whyNot.2: An attorney can be consulted, so the IMCA duty does not arise.
